stories.title: Cyber Risk Management Firm Signs Five-Year Renewal of Midtown Offices
stories.excerpt: JLL arepresented SecurityScorecard, a global leader in cyber risk intelligence, in a five-year renewal of its full-floor headquarters at 1140 Ave. of the Americas in Midtown Manhattan. A tenant since 2023, the company occupies 8,475 square feet across a full floor featuring a large private outdoor terrace and collaborative workspace. The Cushman & Wakefield team of Josh Kuriloff, Matthias Li, Heather Thomas, Pierce Hance and Nicole Estevez represented the landlord in leasing negotiations. JLL Managing Director Valentin Stobetsky represented SecurityScorecard. “1140 Avenue of the Americas offers everything a fast-growing technology company like SecurityScorecard is looking for,” said Stobetsky. “It has a premier Midtown location, outstanding transit access, modern amenities and a unique full-floor office with an expansive private outdoor terrace that enhances the employee experience. It’s an ideal environment for attracting top talent and supporting the company’s next phase of growth.” The post Cyber Risk Management Firm Signs Five-Year Renewal of Midtown Offices appeared first on Connect CRE.

stories.summary: SecurityScorecard, a cyber risk intelligence firm, renewed its full-floor headquarters at 1140 Avenue of the Americas in Midtown Manhattan for five years. The company occupies 8,475 square feet featuring a private outdoor terrace and collaborative workspace. The renewal reflects strong tenant confidence in premium Midtown office space and the property's appeal to fast-growing tech companies.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily development. However, sustained tech employer presence and expansion in Manhattan CBD reinforces office-to-residential intra-city migration patterns; signals continued professional-class job concentration in Manhattan that underpins demand for luxury/Class A rental housing in adjacent residential submarkets (TriBeCa, Nolita, Upper West Side).

stories.title: Data Centers Push Into Frontier Markets
stories.excerpt: One trend emerging from JLL’s Midyear North America Data Center Report is that developers continue to hit the power wall. This obstacle is stretching timelines in established hubs, encouraging developers to examine space in areas that were once outside of the industry’s main hubs. Working the Energy Crisis Sean Farney The power challenge raises the question of where developers can find the needed electricity to get new centers off the ground. JLL Vice President of Data Center Strategy Sean Farney told Connect CRE that developers are experimenting with alternative power solutions to bypass grid constraints and improve development timelines. Utilities are directing developers toward co-located generation and on-site battery storage, while microgrids are also a potential solution for addressing grid constraints. Those microgrids, however, remain under regulatory scrutiny. Direct partnerships with utilities are also becoming more common. Despite these efforts, long interconnection timelines remain a problem. Farney said new Commonwealth Edison projects in Chicago have four- to five-year delivery timelines, along with letter-of-credit commitments of approximately $46,000 per megawatt annually for 10 years. “Grid limitations in Columbus, OH, are pushing users to secondary markets with available capacity,” he added. Mining the Frontier The reports refer to these secondary regions as “frontier markets,” noting that 77% of capacity under construction is located in such areas. These markets offer several advantages in addition to greater power availability. They provide builder-friendly regulatory environments, enough land to accommodate large campuses, lower operating costs and room for long-term expansion. Farney said grid constraints in Columbus are pushing overflow development toward the Ohio cities of Van Wert, Lima and Canton. bullets: Power constraints in established data center hubs pushing developers toward secondary markets and alternative energy solutions
Chicago Commonwealth Edison projects face 4–5 year interconnection timelines; $46K/MW annual letter-of-credit commitments over 10 years
Columbus OH and other secondary markets gaining developer interest due to grid availability; microgrids and on-site generation emerging solutions
stories.summary: Data center developers are hitting power supply constraints in established hubs like Chicago, prompting exploration of frontier markets and alternative energy solutions including on-site generation, battery storage, and microgrids. ComEd projects in Chicago face 4–5 year delivery timelines with substantial annual LC commitments. Developers are increasingly examining secondary markets with greater grid capacity.
stories.impact: Secondary market data center development signals upstream demand for workforce housing in markets like Columbus, Raleigh, Phoenix, and Dallas that offer power availability. Multifamily developers should monitor data center pipeline announcements in secondary metros—they often precede or coincide with employment growth and inbound migration, creating lead-time arbitrage opportunities for acquisition and development in those submarkets.

stories.title: Lincoln Property, SVP Complete Redevelopment of Playa Vista Creative Campus
stories.excerpt: Lincoln Property Company and Strategic Value Partners, LLC, have completed the redevelopment of The Bluffs at Playa Vista, a 500,000-square-foot Class A office campus in the heart of Playa Vista’s live-work-play community. More than 57,000 square feet in new leases were recently signed at The Bluffs ahead of the repositioning’s completion, including The Honest Company’s 38,240-square-foot headquarters relocation and Thrive Causemetics’ 19,076-square-foot office lease. “As one of the largest contiguous Class A offering in West Los Angeles, The Bluffs presented a compelling opportunity to reimagine a large-scale asset in a best-in-class Playa Vista location with strong fundamentals already in place,” said Rob Kane, senior EVP at Lincoln. “Through comprehensive capital improvements, we transformed the campus with a more hospitality-inspired approach centered on quality shared spaces, stronger indoor-outdoor connectivity, and a workplace experience authentic to Playa Vista’s innovation-driven identity.” Located at 12121 and 12181 Bluff Creek Dr., The Bluffs is a two-building creative campus offering flexible, dual-core floor plates up to 50,000 square feet. stories.summary: Lincoln Property Company and Strategic Value Partners completed redevelopment of The Bluffs at Playa Vista, a 500,000-square-foot Class A office campus. More than 57,000 square feet of new leases were signed ahead of completion, including The Honest Company's headquarters relocation and Thrive Causemetics' office lease. The repositioning centered on enhanced shared spaces and workplace experience aligned with Playa Vista's innovation culture.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance, but office consolidation in Playa Vista (and Honest Company HQ relocation from elsewhere) signals localized job agglomeration in West LA submarket. Strong office absorption in lifestyle-driven mixed-use district reinforces adjacent residential demand; multifamily developers should monitor other large employer relocations to West LA nodes (Marina, Brentwood) for signs of sustained office-driven housing demand growth.

stories.title: L.A. County Investment Sales Jump 28% in July Thanks to Multifamily
stories.excerpt: Commercial real estate investment sales accelerated across Los Angeles County in July, with multifamily accounting for the majority of capital deployed. About 7.25 million square feet of commercial property traded for $2.1 billion last month, NAI Capital reported Thursday, citing CoStar data. Compared to July 2025, almost 22 percent more square footage traded hands during July to make for a 28.5 percent jump in dollar volume. Compared with July 2024, sales volume climbed 75 percent. The gains came despite elevated borrowing costs, with long-term Treasury yields remaining near multiyear highs. Multifamily dominated, with 3.43 million square feet changing hands for $1.22 billion — accounting for 58 percent of all investment during the month in L.A. County. Sales volume increased 55 percent since last year, and almost 166 percent compared to July 2024. Average pricing rose 28.7 percent to $376 per square foot. People look at the Los Angeles skyline from Griffith Observatory. PHOTO: Matt McNulty - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images Retail also posted broad gains. About 1.23 million square feet sold for $402 million, pushing dollar volume up 40 percent from a year ago, and nearly doubling the July 2024 total. Retail square footage traded has climbed 135 percent over the same two-year period. Industrial faces a more complicated environment. About 1.33 million square feet traded in July, which is almost 71 percent higher since 2025, but dollar volume remained about flat at $214 million, and average pricing fell 3.6 percent to $273 per square foot. Office was the only major property type to decline in both sales volume and square footage. About 1.26 million square feet sold for $262 million, down 9.7 percent and 23.4 percent, respectively, from July 2025. Average pricing dropped 23.5 percent to $250 per square foot. Multifamily sales volume surged 55% year-over-year and 166% compared to July 2024, with average pricing rising 28.7% to $376 per square foot. stories.impact: Strong LA County multifamily transaction activity and 28.7% YoY price appreciation signal investor confidence and capital availability despite rate environment. Market fundamentals (pricing, volume, buyer appetite) support development feasibility; multifamily developers should expedite underwriting and financing for LA County projects to capitalize on investor competition and pricing momentum before cap rate compression moderates. Monitor whether pricing gains are driven by coastal/primary submarkets (Santa Monica, Playa Vista, Downtown) or spreading to secondary markets.

stories.title: New York City’s Technology Labor Market Has Surpassed San Francisco: Report
stories.excerpt: It’s official. New York is employing more tech workers than the San Francisco Bay area. According to an annual CBRE report on North American tech talent, the New York metropolitan area’s tech workforce reached 394,300 in 2025. The stat marks an 8.4 percent increase from 2022 that added 30,640 jobs. Meanwhile, San Francisco’s tech employment fell by 6 percent over the same period, totaling 375,730 jobs in 2025. This is the first time in the report’s 13-year history that the Big Apple has come out ahead. The city’s diversified job market helped set it apart, Colin Yasukochi, executive director of CBRE’s tech insights center, told Commercial Observer. “What really pushed New York past the San Francisco Bay Area has been the job reductions that we’ve seen [in San Francisco], with a lot of the announced layoffs, and the fact that New York has continued to grow,” Yasukochi said. San Francisco remains in North America’s top spot for its pool of tech talent, however, ranked across 13 metrics. The report, which analyzed the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and LinkedIn data, found that tech jobs make up more than 10 percent of total employment in San Francisco, compared to just 4.2 percent in New York. But a whopping 61 percent of San Francisco’s tech talent works directly in the tech industry, according to CBRE’s report, leaving its general labor market vulnerable. In New York City, just 34 percent of its tech workers work within the industry, while 21 percent work in tech roles in finance, insurance and real estate industries (otherwise known as FIRE). “[That] has given New York resilience from the tech downturn that broadly started in 2022, in terms of employment,” Yasukochi said. “But, obviously, with the artificial intelligence industry coming into play, that’s turned around quite substantially in the last year.” Yasukochi added that New York also benefits from a massive university infrastructure and lower wages than San Francisco, on average, for
bullets: NYC metro tech workforce reached 394,300 in 2025 (+8.4% since 2022); surpassed San Francisco for first time

stories.summary: New York City's metropolitan tech workforce reached 394,300 in 2025, marking an 8.4% gain since 2022 and surpassing San Francisco Bay Area's 375,730 tech workers (down 6% over the same period) for the first time in 13 years. NYC's diversified economy and sustained job growth, contrasted with San Francisco's announced layoffs and reductions, drove the milestone.
stories.impact: Significant demand signal for multifamily in NYC: tech employment growth (+30,640 net jobs since 2022) adds high-earning renter cohort and strengthens rental demand across Manhattan (Flatiron, Midtown South, Lower East Side) and waterfront/emerging tech nodes (Long Island City, Williamsburg, Brooklyn Tech Triangle). Conversely, Bay Area tech contraction may soften rental demand in San Francisco, Oakland, and Peninsula submarkets; multifamily developers should redirect acquisition focus toward NYC-area sites and recalibrate San Francisco development underwriting downward.

stories.title: Principal Financial Group Loans $32M to Refi Queens Shopping Center
stories.excerpt: An affiliate of Mattone Investors secured $32 million to refinance Springnex Plaza, a 96,028-square-foot shopping center anchored by a Stop & Shop supermarket in the Queens neighborhood of Springfield Gardens. Principal Financial Group provided the debt, while Northmarq’s Robert Delitsky and Charles Cotsalas arranged the transaction. Delitsky noted in a statement that Mattone Investors first developed Springnex Plaza six years ago and “have done a fabulous job maintaining very strong occupancy” since then. “Supermarket-anchored shopping centers like Springnex Plaza will continue to attract very strong lender interest in today’s market,” Cotsalas added in the same statement. Located at 134-40 Springfield Boulevard, Springnex Plaza sits on 5.58 acres of land and is 100 percent occupied. Besides Stop & Shop, tenants include an IHOP, fashion retailer Ashley Stewart and Northwell Health GoHealth Urgent Care. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.

stories.summary: An affiliate of Mattone Investors obtained a $32 million refinance from Principal Financial Group for Springnex Plaza, a 96,028-square-foot shopping center in Queens' Springfield Gardens neighborhood anchored by Stop & Shop. The property is 100% occupied and includes IHOP, Ashley Stewart, and Northwell Health GoHealth Urgent Care. The refinance affirms supermarket-anchored retail's resilience and lender support.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact. However, strong occupancy and financing availability in Queens retail signals economic health and foot-traffic vitality in outer-borough neighborhoods; retail stability supports adjacent residential demand. Multifamily developers should monitor retail fundamentals in Queens markets (Springfield Gardens, Jamaica, Elmhurst) as complementary amenity and anchor demand signal for nearby apartment developments.

stories.title: Data Center Development Has Domestic Materials Manufacturers Working Overtime
stories.excerpt: Development in the U.S. saw spotty progress in the first half of 2026 with costs of materials continuing to climb and asset classes with only the highest returns being built. That means data centers, power infrastructure, advanced manufacturing and pharmaceutical production are taking off, while office, retail and higher education on a national level lag way behind, due, in large part, to President Donald Trump’s ongoing tariff policies, according to a Skanska report. But just because there is a lull in some sectors does not mean supply chains for materials aren’t working at full capacity, Tom Park, vice president of national strategic supply chain at Skanska, told Commercial Observer. “The market is hot and cold right now — hot and warm may be a better way to say it — so what stands out is that we’re seeing a lot of project activity around data centers, semiconductor, life sciences,” Park said in an interview. “There’s really a lot of unprecedented demand in the mechanical, electrical, plumbing and steel space driving up lead times and cost.” Some factors causing these supply chain hemorrhages are Section 338 tariffs on Canada, delays on petrochemical import ships through the Strait of Hormuz, and domestic materials priced higher simply because of the supply and demand constraints. Tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper in particular are driving prices up. “What happens with tariffs is that it really raises the opportunity for domestic producers to raise their prices,” Park said. “For steel, aluminum and copper, the tariffs really have increased pricing on all those materials and derivative products because the foreign competition obviously has that tariff to overcome.” Lead times for material deliveries have increased from 24 to 36 weeks to 40 to 50 weeks, indicating to Park that metal mills and fabricators are running at full capacity. bullets: H1 2026 U.S. development uneven; data centers, advanced manufacturing, pharma accelerating; office, retail, higher ed lagging due to Trump tariffs
Mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and steel lead times and costs climbing; unprecedented demand from data center and semiconductor projects

stories.summary: U.S. development in the first half of 2026 showed uneven progress, with data centers, advanced manufacturing, and pharmaceutical production surging while office, retail, and higher education lag due to tariff policies. Data center and semiconductor projects are driving unprecedented demand for MEP and steel, extending lead times and inflating material costs across the supply chain.
stories.impact: Rising material and labor costs directly compress multifamily development feasibility and underwriting returns in H2 2026 and 2027. Developers should lock in MEP and steel pricing now; expect 10–15% cost inflation on construction. Tariff-driven cost escalation may push multifamily starts into infill/redevelopment categories with lower material intensity (adaptive reuse, modular construction) and force geographic shift toward markets with favorable zoning and lower land costs to absorb cost deltas.

stories.title: Azora, Vizcaya Capital Flip Coconut Grove Office Building for $62M
stories.excerpt: Just a year after buying a boutique office building in Miami’s coveted Coconut Grove neighborhood, Azora Private Solutions and Vizcaya Capital sold it for a nearly $15 million gain. The five-story property at 3250 Mary Street, called the Grove at 3250 Mary, sold for $62.3 million, according to the brokers who represented the sellers, Berkadia’s Omar Morales and Jaret Turkell. The joint venture had purchased the 80,000-square-foot building for $47.5 million last September. Records show the buyer is an entity tied to El-Ad National Properties, the Boca Raton-based division of Israeli billionaire Isaac Tshuva’s El-Ad Group. “Coconut Grove continues to distinguish itself as one of South Florida’s strongest real estate markets, driven by exceptional demand from luxury residential buyers and high-net-worth office users,” Morales said in a statement. “That demand, combined with limited supply, continues to attract remarkable investment to the neighborhood.” In recent years, Coconut Grove has attracted a slew of billionaires, including Google’s billionaire founder Larry Page, who spent about $170 million assembling a residential compound last year. The residential acquisitions have fueled demand for luxury office space nearby. The acquisition of the 1982-built, 1.3-acre site office building marks somewhat of a deviation for El-Ad National, which has typically focused on residential and mixed-use development. It also comes just four months after the developer purchased a nearby, low-rise condo building for $45.5 million, which will likely be redeveloped. Earlier this month, up north in Fort Lauderdale, the firm bought an oceanfront hotel for $60 million. A representative for El-Ad Group was not immediately available for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialoserver.com.
bullets: Azora, Vizcaya sell Grove at 3250 Mary (80,000 sq ft, Coconut Grove office) for $62.3M; $14.8M gain in one year

stories.summary: Azora Private Solutions and Vizcaya Capital sold the Grove at 3250 Mary, an 80,000-square-foot office building in Coconut Grove, for $62.3 million—a $14.8 million gain just one year after purchase at $47.5 million. The buyer is an entity tied to El-Ad National Properties. The quick flip reflects strong demand from luxury residential buyers and high-net-worth office tenants in Coconut Grove.
stories.impact: Coconut Grove office-to-mixed-use conversion signal: tight office supply and investor competition for renovated creative office in Miami's lifestyle district suggests underlying thesis that Coconut Grove office will convert to residential or mixed-use within 3–5 years. Multifamily developers should identify Coconut Grove office buildings with expiring leases or below-market tenancy as conversion candidates; comparable sales growth ($15M gain in 12 months) implies strong investor appetite for repositioned residential product in the submarket.
